pack.description: Listen and Choose a Response — single spoken prompts with four written replies.
pack.copyright_policy: Original synthetic content. No operational ETS item copied.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Weren't you planning to submit the application yesterday?

options: I was, but the website stopped working.
You can submit it at the front desk.
exercises.explanation: A negative question asks for confirmation of a plan; the reply confirms the plan and explains why it did not happen. The other options repeat words (application, yesterday, submit) without answering.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Do you know if the chemistry lab is open on Sundays?

options: Yes, I took chemistry last year.
I think it's only open on weekdays.
The lab report is due on Sunday.
exercises.explanation: An embedded yes/no question about opening days; only the reply about weekdays answers it.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I can't believe the professor postponed the exam again.

options: Well, at least we have more time to review.
I believe she teaches two sections.
exercises.explanation: The speaker expresses frustration; a natural reply offers a positive perspective. "Believe" and "again" in other options are word traps.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Would you mind if I borrowed your notes from Tuesday's lecture?

options: Not at all — I'll send you a copy tonight.
Yes, the lecture was on Tuesday.
exercises.explanation: "Would you mind…?" is answered "Not at all" to grant permission. "Yes" would literally mean refusal.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Why did they move the career fair to the gym?

options: Because the ballroom is being renovated.
I'm going to the gym later.
exercises.explanation: A why-question needs a reason. "It starts at ten" answers when; "Most employers will be there" answers who.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: You haven't seen my blue folder anywhere, have you?

options: Is it the one you left in the seminar room?
exercises.explanation: A tag question asking for help locating something; answering with a helpful clarifying question is natural.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I was wondering whether you'd had a chance to look at my draft.

options: Not yet, but I'll get to it by Friday.
I had a chance to travel.
exercises.explanation: "I was wondering whether…" is a polite indirect request for information; the reply gives status and a commitment.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: If I were you, I'd talk to the advisor before dropping the course.

options: You're right — I'll make an appointment this week.
The course was dropped last year.
exercises.explanation: "If I were you, I'd…" is advice; accepting it is the coherent response.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: How long does it usually take to get a reply from the housing office?

options: About a week, in my experience.
exercises.explanation: "How long" asks for duration. "Usually by email" answers how, not how long.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Shouldn't we have heard back from the journal by now?

options: We should hear the concert tonight.
Their reviews often take three months, so it's not unusual.
exercises.explanation: The speaker expresses worry about a delay; the answer reassures by explaining that the delay is normal.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Could you tell me where the printing station is on this floor?

options: It's at the end of the hall, past the elevators.
Yes, I printed it this morning.
exercises.explanation: An embedded where-question asks for a location.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I'm afraid the seminar is already full.

options: Is there a waiting list I could join?
exercises.explanation: "I'm afraid…" softens bad news; it does not express fear. Asking about a waiting list is the logical follow-up.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: That presentation could hardly have gone better, could it?

options: It could have been much better.
Yes, it was hard to hear.
exercises.explanation: "Could hardly have gone better" means it went extremely well; agreeing with the negative tag uses "No" + praise.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Which of these two textbooks would you recommend for a beginner?

options: Both books are on the shelf.
The thinner one — it explains the basics more clearly.
exercises.explanation: "Which…?" requires choosing one and ideally justifying it.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I've been meaning to ask — are you still looking for a roommate?

options: Actually, I found someone last week.
I'm looking at the room now.
exercises.explanation: The question asks whether the search continues; "I found someone" answers no, politely.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Not that I'm complaining, but the heating in the lab has been off all week.

options: I'll report it to facilities this afternoon.
The lab has been busy all week.
exercises.explanation: "Not that I'm complaining, but…" introduces a complaint. The appropriate reply addresses the problem.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: When are office hours this week?

exercises.explanation: "When" asks for a time; distractors answer where, how long, how often.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: You might want to double-check the figures before sending the report.

options: Good point — I'll go through them again.
I already sent you a figure.
exercises.explanation: "You might want to…" is a polite suggestion that something may be wrong; accepting it is appropriate.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Had I known the bus was cancelled, I would have left earlier.

options: Didn't you get the text alert this morning?
exercises.explanation: The inverted conditional means "I didn't know". The reply asks why she wasn't informed. "You left very early" contradicts her statement.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Is it okay to bring food into the reading room?

options: Only covered drinks are allowed, I think.
I'm reading a book about food.
Bring it to the front desk.
exercises.explanation: Permission question; the reply states the rule (food not allowed, covered drinks only).

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I can't make the study group tonight after all.

options: No problem — we'll send you a summary.
Tonight is after the study group.
exercises.explanation: "After all" signals a change of plan; a supportive response accepts the cancellation.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I wouldn't be surprised if the deadline got pushed back again.

options: Neither would I — it's happened twice already.
Push it back to the shelf.
exercises.explanation: Agreeing with a negative statement uses "Neither would I".

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Who's in charge of booking the speakers for the conference?

options: That would be Marcus, from the events committee.
exercises.explanation: "Who" requires a person.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Didn't the department say the scholarship results would be out today?

options: Yes, but apparently there's been a delay.
The scholarship is out of the department.
exercises.explanation: Negative question seeking confirmation; the reply confirms and adds new information.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Given how long the line is, it might be quicker to renew the permit online.

options: Good idea — I'll do that from my phone.
I've given my permit to someone.
exercises.explanation: The speaker suggests an alternative; accepting it fits. "The line is very quick" contradicts the situation.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Do you happen to have a charger I could use for a few minutes?

options: Sorry, mine doesn't fit that model.
It happened a few minutes ago.
exercises.explanation: A polite request; a polite refusal with a reason is coherent.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I'm thinking of switching my major to environmental science.

options: Science is my major too, years ago.
exercises.explanation: Sharing a plan invites interest; asking about the reason continues the conversation naturally.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I'd have thought the results would be more conclusive, considering the sample size.

options: Me too — maybe there's too much variation in the data.
exercises.explanation: The speaker expresses surprise that a large sample gave weak results; the reply agrees and offers a possible explanation.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: How much does it cost to join the hiking club?

options: Twenty dollars for the whole year.
exercises.explanation: "How much" + cost asks for a price.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Let me know if there's anything I can do to help with the move.

options: Thanks — could you bring some boxes on Saturday?
exercises.explanation: An offer of help; accepting it with a concrete request is natural.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: So much for finishing the project before the break.

options: I know — we underestimated how long the analysis would take.
The break is so much fun.
exercises.explanation: "So much for X" means X did not happen as hoped. The reply acknowledges the failed plan.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Are we supposed to cite the lecture slides or the original articles?

options: The professor prefers the original sources.
The slides were supposed to be shorter.
I suppose the articles are long.
We cited the lecture last week.
exercises.explanation: An either/or question; the answer chooses one option.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: You look exhausted — were you up late again?

options: I was finishing my lab report until two.
exercises.explanation: The question asks whether the person stayed up late; the reply confirms with a reason.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: It's not as though the instructions were unclear.

options: True — I just didn't read them carefully enough.
exercises.explanation: "It's not as though X" means X is false: the instructions were clear. The reply concedes the point.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Where should I leave the signed forms?

exercises.explanation: "Where" asks for a place.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I hope you don't mind me saying so, but your conclusion feels a bit rushed.

options: Not at all — I ran out of time. What would you add?
exercises.explanation: Polite criticism; accepting it and asking for advice is the appropriate response.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Funny you should mention the internship — I was just about to apply.

options: Really? The deadline is tomorrow, so don't wait.
exercises.explanation: "Funny you should mention" signals coincidence, not humor; the reply builds on her plan.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: Has anyone told the new students about the safety training?

options: I emailed them the schedule yesterday.
exercises.explanation: The reply confirms the students were informed.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: I could have sworn the meeting was in the east building.

options: It was, until they changed it this morning.
I could meet you in the east.
The east building was sworn in.
exercises.explanation: "I could have sworn" = I was sure (but I may be wrong). The reply explains the change.

audio.speaker: Speaker
audio.text: We're running short of chairs for the workshop.

options: I'll grab a few from the room next door.
exercises.explanation: A statement of a problem invites an offer to solve it.
